title: Python Lists: The Beginner's Blueprint
summary: A dense, two-page study guide covering the core mechanics of Python lists, from creation and indexing to slicing and mutation pitfalls.

chapters.title: Creation & Indexing Mechanics
points: Definition: A list is a mutable, ordered sequence of objects stored in a dynamic array.
Syntax: Create empty with [] or with elements like fruits = ['apple', 'banana', 'cherry'].
Mechanism: Internally, Python uses a pointer array; elements are references, not copies.
Indexing: Access items via zero-based positive indices: fruits[0] returns 'apple'.
Negative Indexing: Access from the end using negative indices: fruits[-1] returns 'cherry'.
Example: my_list = [10, 20, 30]; print(my_list[-2]) outputs 20.
Error Handling: Accessing an out-of-bounds index raises an IndexError, not None.
Comparison: Unlike tuples, lists allow modification of elements after creation.
Mistake: Assuming indices start at 1; always remember index 0 is the first element.
Mistake: Confusing negative index -1 (last item) with -len(list) (first item).
Trade-off: Dynamic resizing has amortized O(1) append cost but O(n) for middle insertions.
Summary: Lists are mutable, ordered, and accessed via 0-based or negative indices.

chapters.title: Slicing, Mutation & Pitfalls
points: Slicing: Extract sublists with list[start:stop:step]; stop is exclusive.
Example: nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]; nums[1:4] returns [2, 3, 4].
Mechanism: Slicing always creates a new list (shallow copy), not a view.
Append: Adds a single object as the last element; O(1) amortized time.
Extend: Iterates over an iterable and adds each element individually; O(k) time.
Comparison: my_list.append([1, 2]) adds a nested list; my_list.extend([1, 2]) adds 1 and 2.
Mistake: Using extend with a string, which splits it into individual characters.
Mistake: Shared reference mutation; if b = a, then b.append(1) also changes a.
Fix: Use a = b.copy() or a = b[:] to create an independent copy before modifying.
Complexity: Slicing is O(k) where k is the slice length; copying is O(n).
Practical Tip: Use list comprehension for transformations instead of manual loops.
Summary: Master slicing for extraction, distinguish append/extend, and always copy before mutating shared lists.
